papers.title: T cell transcriptomes in simulated microgravity in vivo
papers.abstract: Spaceflight exposes astronauts to a combination of stressors, among which microgravity remains the least well characterized at the level of human immune cell function. We examined the in vivo effect of long-term simulated microgravity (SMG) on T cell transcriptomes in ten healthy male volunteers who completed a three-week dry immersion protocol without countermeasures. Peripheral blood was collected at five time points covering a pre-immersion baseline (day -7), three intra-exposure time points (days 7, 14 and 21) and a recovery time point one week after the end of exposure (day 28). CD3+ T cells were isolated and analysed by RNA-seq, with differential expression assessed per volunteer and KEGG pathway enrichment used to identify the most affected gene networks. SMG was associated with transcript-level changes in genes mapping to key molecular pathways, including those involved in cell proliferation, cell-cycle regulation, maintenance of genome integrity, and oncogenic and tumour-suppressor networks. Hub genes shared across the most significant pathways were differentially expressed in the majority of volunteers. A notable finding was pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity: samples clustered primarily by volunteer identity, yet a coordinated temporal shift during exposure and a partial return toward baseline by day 28 were detectable across donors, and these changes occurred in the absence of detectable systemic inflammation. These results indicate that SMG is associated with altered T cell transcriptional programs in vivo and that the response is sufficiently variable between individuals to favor personalized rather than uniform countermeasure strategies.

papers.title: Dynamic allocation of MurJ coordinates bacterial growth and division
papers.abstract: Rod-shaped bacteria grow by inserting peptidoglycan into the lateral cell wall during elongation and into the septal cell wall during division. These two modes of growth are driven by distinct peptidoglycan synthesis machineries that consume the shared precursor Lipid II and must be coordinated so that cell enlargement remains matched to division. However, how cells spatially allocate this shared precursor, and whether Lipid II translocation itself contributes to this coordi-nation, remain unclear. Here we show that the spatial distribution of the essential Lipid II flippase MurJ coordinates this balance in Escherichia coli. Increasing nonseptal MurJ abundance shifted cell-wall synthesis toward elongation and reduced septal synthesis. Single-molecule tracking revealed that MurJ diffuses throughout the membrane but is transiently captured at the division site, rather than stably incorporated into the septal synthesis machinery. This recruitment requires active septal cell-wall synthesis, but not ongoing Lipid II synthesis or flipping, indicating that MurJ recruitment is coupled to the active synthesis machinery rather than to substrate availability or transport. Thus, activation of septal synthesis creates transient MurJ capture at the division site, providing a mechanism to preferentially supply Lipid II for septal growth during cytokinesis. These findings reveal a capture-and-release mechanism that dynamically enriches MurJ at active division sites and thereby coordinates elongation and division in bacterial cells.

papers.title: Sexual interactions and local selection shape reproductive gene diversity and divergence
papers.abstract: Genes involved in genotype x genotype coevolution display unique patterns of nucleotide diversity and population divergence. In Drosophila melanogaster, Sex Peptide is a key sperm competition gene that is an outlier for both pi within populations and Fst between populations. This pattern is not predicted by current theoretical expectations of selective sweeps highlighting the need to develop predictions to identify genes experiencing balancing selection. We compared pi and FST in D. melanogaster populations to identify other genes following a co-evolutionary model that generates divergence and diversity. Multiple male and female genes that interact with Sex Peptide exhibited elevated FST x pi values. Genome-wide analyses also revealed an enrichment of genes critical for neuronal development, pointing to courtship evolution. Specifically, fruitless, its interacting genes, and a female behavior gene were identified as outliers. These parallel findings indicate that both sperm competition and mating behaviors are subject to co-evolutionary selection.

papers.title: Nematode species differ in susceptibility and response to the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora
papers.abstract: Fungal predators of nematodes are widespread and represent promising candidates for biological control of parasitic nematodes. However, the behavioural and molecular mechanisms underlying nematode-fungus interactions remain poorly understood, especially for nematodes other than Caenorhabditis elegans. We investigated the interactions between the nematode-trapping fungus Arthrobotrys oligospora and three nematode species: (i) free-living C. elegans, (ii) fig-associated C. inopinata, and (iii) the free-living adult life cycle stage of the gastrointestinal parasite Strongyloides ratti. A. oligospora trapped S. ratti more efficiently than either C. elegans or C. inopinata. Behavioural analyses revealed species-specific differences in nematode locomotion. S. ratti moved slower, travelled shorter distances and showed lower displacement than Caenorhabditis spp. To test whether locomotion influences fungal trapping, we examined eight C. elegans mutants with hyper- or hypoactive locomotory phenotypes. Although both groups moved at similar speeds, hyperactive mutants showed greater displacement, which positively correlated with trap formation but did not explain trapping efficiency by A. oligospora. We investigated the fungal response during interaction with the three nematodes. Exposure to S. ratti, but not to Caenorhabditis spp, resulted in reduced sporulation and differential expression of sporulation-associated genes. In nematodes, myosin-related genes responded to A. oligospora in a species-specific manner, including upregulation in C. elegans and downregulation in S. ratti. These transcriptional changes may reflect alterations in muscle structure, including reduction in dense body and mitochondrial size in Caenorhabditis species but not S. ratti during A. oligospora exposure. Together, our findings demonstrate that both fungal and nematode responses are nematode species dependent. These results improve our understanding of nematode-fungus interactions and highlight the importance of nematode species when developing nematode-trapping fungi as a biological control agent.

papers.title: Human lymphatic organoids reconstruct convergent developmental routes to functional lymphatic vessels
papers.abstract: The lymphatic vasculature maintains fluid balance, regulates immune surveillance, and supports tissue repair, yet how human lymphatic vessels arise and acquire specialized functions remains poorly understood. Here, guided by single-cell and spatial analyses of human embryos, we found that both lateral plate and paraxial mesoderm converge on venous endothelial intermediates with cardinal vein-like characteristics prior to lymphatic specification. Informed by these developmental trajectories, we generated three-dimensional lymphatic organoids from human pluripotent stem cells through two distinct mesodermal routes. The organoids formed capillary-like vascular networks with emerging button-like junctions and distinct endothelial and stromal programs. The lymphatic organoids were transcriptionally benchmarked to human fetal lymphatic endothelium. The organoids supported immune-cell interactions and antigen accumulation and, following transplantation, exhibited interstitial tracer uptake and transport. These findings establish a platform for investigating how distinct developmental origins shape human lymphatic specification, vascular organization, and function, with applications to lymphatic disease modeling and tissue repair.

papers.title: Hijacking Cellular S-Acylation with Molecular Assemblies Rewires Oncogenic Signaling
papers.abstract: KRAS-mutant cancers are generally treated by suppressing oncogenic signaling. Here, we investigated whether endogenous lipidation machinery could instead be used to spatially perturb that signaling. The thioester-bearing peptide precursor Stb-DPhe-DPhe-SAc (1) potently reduced PANC-1 cell viability and formed a palmitoylated product in treated cells. Synthetic palmitoylated 1 displayed increased assembly propensity, while fluorescent analogue 2 accumulated at the Golgi in a 2-bromopalmitate-sensitive manner. Compound 1 increased plasma-membrane-associated KRAS staining and ERK/AKT phosphorylation and induced pronounced LC3B and p62 remodeling. Inhibition of palmitoylation suppressed Golgi accumulation, attenuated the LC3B response, and rescued cell viability. These findings support a model in which cellular S-acylation drives organelle-localized molecular assembly that perturbs KRAS localization, oncogenic signaling, and associated stress responses. This work identifies endogenous lipidation machinery as a synthetic handle for spatial control of cancer signaling.

papers.title: Metformin lowers HMGA1a and RBM3 protein in breast cancer cells, and its effect on ESR1 splicing depends on cell density and exposure time
papers.abstract: The ESR1 gene produces ER46, an N-terminally truncated isoform generated by skipping of exon 1, which is reduced in tamoxifen-resistant breast cancer cells. We have reported that metformin moves the ratio of full-length ER to ER46 in opposite directions in MCF-7 cells and their tamoxifen-resistant subline TAMR1, and that metformin reduces TAMR1 xenograft growth (Harada et al., Am J Pharm Health Res 2022;10(11)). That report leaves two questions open: whether the effect is dosedependent and stable across culture conditions, and what splicing factor might carry it. Here we report the experiments that bear on both. Across a full dose range from 0.25 to 5 mM at high seeding density, metformin produced no consistent change in the full-length share of ESR1 transcript in either line: densitometry of the gel gave 42%, 43%, 42%, 43%, 45% and 48% in MCF-7 cells and 55%, 44%, 52%, 47%, 68% and 43% in TAMR1 cells. The reported shift therefore depends on the seeding density used, and the comparison that produced it is not reproduced at high density. At low density the MCF-7 response persisted to 48 h (52%, 62% and 68% at 0, 2.5 and 5 mM). Metformin lowered HMGA1a protein in MCF-7 cells and showed the same tendency in TAMR1 cells, at both seeding densities, and lowered RBM3 protein in TAMR1 cells at 24 and 48 h. HMGA1a is the factor we previously showed to generate ER46 by trapping U1 snRNP at an upstream pseudo-5' splice site, so a fall in HMGA1a predicts less ER46, the opposite of what was seen in TAMR1 cells at low density. The fall in RBM3, the protein through which metformin alters splicing in myotonic dystrophy, is the more plausible candidate. RT-PCR of the xenograft tumours from the earlier study detected full-length ESR1 transcript in the untreated and tamoxifen-plus-metformin groups but not in the singleagent groups, with amplification failing in several lanes; these panels do not separate the treatments. Taken together, the direction of the metformin effect on ESR1 splicing is conditional on culture density and does not survive a dose-response test at high density, and HMGA1a is unlikely to be the factor that carries it.

papers.title: Cytomegalovirus Infection in Human Cortical Organoids Induces Unique Developmental and Viral Substates
papers.abstract: Human Cytomegalovirus (HCMV) is a ubiquitous {beta}-herpesvirus with exposure resulting in a life-long infection. Severe HCMV disease can occur in conditions of insufficient immunity, and this includes congenital infection. Infection of the developing brain can cause severe birth defects including microcephaly and sensorineural hearing loss. Also, increasing evidence suggests the contribution of HCMV infection in adult CNS diseases. Studying HCMV replication and its impact on CNS is restricted by host tropism and anatomy. In these studies, we define the impact of infection on healthy iPSC-derived cortical organoids using single cell RNA sequencing. We uncovered 16 cell type clusters in uninfected tissues using the Human Neural Organoid Cell Atlas. Following infection by HCMV expressing GFP, several clusters were altered in both GFP-positive and GFP-negative populations, including the likely transition of the Glutamatergic/GABAergic Neuron cluster into a CMV-Infected Cell cluster. Expressions of viral genes varied between cells and cell types, requiring us to introduce a TC (temporal class) indexing score to account for varying stages of infection. This analysis in conjunction with machine learning approaches revealed cells that are likely producing de novo HCMV along with several viral sub-states. Several viral sub-states had significant enrichments of genes involved in epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition, including expression of EpCAM. We independently verified HCMV-induction of EpCAM protein expression in cortical organoids and glutamatergic neurons. In summary, our studies reveal unique features of HCMV infection of cortical organoid tissues, including varying viral sub-states and tropisms, and introduced new approaches to analyze these multi-dimensional complex data sets.

papers.title: A Urinary Metabolomic Signature Associated with Small Intestinal Bacterial Overgrowth in Children with Short Bowel Syndrome
papers.abstract: Direct sampling of the small intestinal microbiome is challenging. Urinary metabolites may offer a noninvasive approach to studying microbial functional activity. We used clinically available gas chromatography/mass spectrometry to profile urinary organic acids in 94 children with short bowel syndrome, comparing those with clinically defined small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO; n=21) with those without SIBO (n=73). SIBO-associated metabolites included microbial fermentation products, dietary derivatives, and host metabolic intermediates. Metabolites enriched in SIBO mapped to aromatic amino acid metabolism, including tryptophan and tyrosine pathways, consistent with altered microbial fermentation. Many associations persisted after adjustment for intestinal anatomy, age, antibiotic exposure, and nutritional composition. These findings identified a urinary metabolic profile associated with clinically defined SIBO in children with short bowel syndrome and support further evaluation of urinary metabolomics as a noninvasive approach to studying small intestinal microbial function.

papers.title: Second-site capsule-locus mutations, not Ade efflux disruption, determine phage susceptibility across an Acinetobacter baumannii transposon mutant panel
papers.abstract: Resistance-Nodulation-Division (RND) efflux pumps have been implicated in phage adsorption in several Gram-negative bacteria, suggesting that AdeABC, AdeFGH and AdeIJK, the three characterised RND efflux systems of multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii, could play a similar role. We tested this hypothesis using five phages (Equilibrator, Taro, AT01, BB02, and AC03) and a panel of 13 A. baumannii strains, including nine AB5075 transposon mutants affecting AdeABC, AdeFGH, or AdeIJK. Host-range testing, efficiency-of-plating assays, capsule-associated density measurements, antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and whole-genome sequencing were performed to assess the relationship between genotype and phage infection. Overall, the data did not support a role for the Ade components as receptors. Phages Equilibrator, Taro and AT01 formed plaques on every strain, and the restricted host ranges of BB02 and AC03 did not correspond to disruption of a particular efflux system. Sequencing instead identified second-site mutations in the KL25 capsule locus in six of the ten AB5075 strains. These included a 1,998-bp deletion affecting wzc, substitutions in mnaA and mnaB, an ISAba13 insertion in a putative glycosyltransferase and a subpopulation-associated frameshift in wzx. AC03 formed plaques on all six strains with capsule-locus changes but on none of the five strains without them. Capsule dependence differed among the other phages: relative to the parental AB5075, infection by these phages, Equilibrator, Taro and BB02, was restricted on the capsule-deficient wzc::T26 strain, whereas AT01 efficiency was only slightly reduced. Insertion-site mapping also distinguished a near-terminal adeK insertion that retained the parental antimicrobial phenotype from an early adeK insertion associated with loss of AdeIJK function. Together, these findings identify capsule-locus variation as the strongest correlation with phage susceptibility in this panel and demonstrate the importance of verifying mutant genomes before assigning phenotypes to their annotated insertions.

papers.title: A Staphylococcus phage recombination cassette that enables recombineering across distant bacteria
papers.abstract: Modifying bacterial genomes with phage recombinases, a process termed recombineering, has enabled precise genome editing, but its reach is limited by host specificity: each new organism generally requires its own recombinase to be identified and optimized. Using known phage recombination genes as synteny anchors, we mined Staphylococcus genomes and recovered a diverse collection of phage recombination cassettes, spanning the RAD52-like annealase superfamily (Sak, Erf) and the RAD51/RecA-like Sak4 family. Functional testing of representatives in S. aureus identified several highly efficient systems that support recombineering. We engineered the most efficient of these into a single-plasmid tool that yields markerless editing in S. aureus in four days. Notably, where other recombineering systems rely on host-specific factors for nuclease evasion and ssDNA loading, this cassette encodes both activities itself: a predicted broad-spectrum nuclease inhibitor and a dedicated single-stranded DNA-binding protein. We therefore tested the cassette across phylogenetically distant hosts, and observed recombination in Streptococcus pyogenes, Enterococcus faecium, Francisella novicida, and Escherichia coli. These results identify a self-sufficient class of phage recombination systems and provide a portable tool for

papers.title: Higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals gate pathobiont expansion through succinate-driven pH modulation
papers.abstract: Despite advances in defining microbiome shifts associated with inflammatory mucosal diseases, the ecological interactions that constrain or facilitate pathobiont expansion remain poorly understood. Using a six-species synthetic oral microbial community and factorial interaction screening, we identified a higher-order interaction governing the growth of the periodontal pathobiont Porphyromonas gingivalis. The core community member Veillonella parvula was the strongest positive determinant of P. gingivalis growth, but this effect was substantially reduced by the health-associated commensal Actinomyces oris. A. oris-mediated antagonism resulted from extracellular acidification and was enhanced under anaerobic conditions. Genetic dissection of A. oris fermentation revealed that lactate dehydrogenase (ldh1) contributes to anaerobic lactate production, but ldh1 deletion only partially relieved P. gingivalis inhibition. Instead, succinate, produced through a succinate dehydrogenase/fumarate reductase pathway (sdh2), emerged as the principal driver of acidification and P. gingivalis suppression. At high cell densities, however, V. parvula consumed both lactate and succinate, reversing acidification and restoring conditions permissive for P. gingivalis growth. To assess the relevance of these interactions in vivo, we analyzed subgingival microbiome from 1,355 adults, including 555 with detectable P. gingivalis. Among these individuals, P. gingivalis abundance was negatively associated with Actinomyces abundance after adjustment for periodontitis severity, whereas this association was attenuated at high V. parvula abundance, consistent with the interaction observed in vitro. Together, these findings identify succinate as a previously unrecognized mediator of interbacterial antagonism and reveal how higher-order metabolic interactions among oral commensals regulate pathobiont expansion through pH modulation, with protective effects shaped by oxygen availability and metabolic cross-feeding.

papers.title: Wild wood mouse gut microbiota are influenced by captivity and cross-fostering
papers.abstract: Background Wild and laboratory animals harbour profoundly different gut microbiota, but how microbiomes shift between these states, and the relative roles of captivity, microbial history, and host identity in shaping that shift, remain unclear. Here, we developed a unique wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus) system comprising free-living mice (Wild:As), a wild-derived colony maintained in captivity for over a decade (Wild-like:As), and a second colony that we generated from the Wild-like:As mice by caesarean rederivation and cross-fostering to laboratory Mus musculus (Lab-like:As). We compared these three Apodemus cohorts with conventional laboratory Mus musculus (Lab:Mm) to ask how microbial diversity, community composition, and functional potential vary across a spectrum of wild-to-laboratory conditions. Results We found that alpha diversity varied substantially among cohorts but showed no consistent wild-to-laboratory trend: Shannon diversity was higher in Lab:Mm and Lab-like:As than in Wild:As and Wild-like:As mice, whereas phylogenetic diversity was similarly high in both the Wild:As and Lab:Mm groups. Community composition more closely reflected cohort histories. Despite over a decade in captivity, Wild-like:As mice remained most similar to Wild:As conspecifics, whereas Lab-like:As mice shifted strongly away from Wild-like:As and toward, but remained distinct from, Lab:Mm mice. The clearest wild-to-laboratory pattern emerged in microbiome consistency: core ASVs (present in [≥]90% of individuals) increased from 9 in Wild:As to 46 in Wild-like:As, 72 in Lab-like:As, and 138 in Lab:Mm mice. Predicted functional potential revealed a further distinction between taxonomic and functional patterns: Wild:As and Wild-like:As microbiomes did not differ significantly, whereas Lab-like:As shifted toward the Lab:Mm state despite remaining taxonomically distinct. Conclusions Together, these results show that laboratory-associated microbiomes do not emerge through simple loss of wild microbial diversity, but through broader reorganisation of community composition, consistency, and predicted functional potential reflecting microbial history and host context. The persistent Wild-like and Lab-like microbiome states within Apodemus provide a powerful experimental system for future timely work testing how microbiome history influences host physiology, resilience, and responses to environmental challenges.

papers.title: Bayesian phylogenetic inference accounting for recombination in whole bacterial genomes
papers.abstract: Recombination is a major evolutionary force in bacteria, and ignoring it distorts phylogenies and can invalidate downstream analyses such as dating. We present ClonalFrame2, a new software for Bayesian phylogenetic inference from whole bacterial genomes that accounts for recombination. It replaces both ClonalFrame and ClonalFrameML while using the same evolutionary model, in which both mutation and recombination events occur on the branches of the clonal genealogy. The locations of recombination events are integrated out of the likelihood using a hidden Markov model, so the algorithm targets only the clonal genealogy and three recombination parameters. Ancestral sequences are recomputed whenever the tree changes and are used to propose efficient topology updates. We validated the method by analysing data-free datasets, which recovered the prior, and by comparing the approximated likelihood with the exact one on simulated data. Across 100 simulated datasets of 100 genomes each, the recombination parameters were accurately recovered, and trees inferred while accounting for recombination were many times more accurate than when ignoring it. In Staphylococcus aureus ST239, we showed that accounting for recombination gave a stronger temporal signal and a more robust dated phylogeny. In Neisseria gonorrhoeae, we identified interesting patterns of clustered recombination events happening repeatedly across the branches of the tree.

papers.title: Orsay virus infection is associated with reduced locomotion and alters cue-dependent food choice in Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Behavioral responses are an important component of host defense; however, most evidence in Caenorhabditis elegans comes from bacterial pathogens. Here, we tested whether infection with Orsay virus (OrV) alters host dispersal and food choice and whether these responses involve the RNA-processing factor EOL-1. When measuring distance travelled over a certain period of time in control and infected wild-type animals, we observed that OrV infection was associated with lower locomotion. Moreover, when presenting infected and control animals with food choices, we observed that infected animals preferred OrV infected food sources only when the alternative was a pure food source, preferring a non-inoculated food source when both control and viral food sources contained a C. elegans filtrate. Moreover, loss of EOL-1 altered baseline locomotion and attenuated the infection-associated reduction detected in the earlier motility assay, while also modifying the food choice response, suggesting that eol-1 contributes to the motility and behavioral changes induced by OrV infection. Collectively, these results support an overall association between OrV infection and reduced host dispersal, whereas its effect on food choice depends on the sensory context. These findings extend infection-associated behavioral responses to a natural viral pathogen and identify eol-1 as a modulator of their expression.

papers.title: Response to azacitidine and the TIM-3 inhibitor, sabatolimab, in MDS and CMML is associated with distinct immune and antigen-presentation states
papers.abstract: Targeting the immune checkpoint TIM-3 is of interest in myeloid neoplasms, yet the hematopoietic and immune changes associated with anti-TIM-3 therapy remain poorly characterized. We used single-cell RNA sequencing to profile bone marrow (BM) and peripheral blood from patients with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) treated with the hypomethylating agent azacitidine combined with sabatolimab, a monoclonal antibody targeting TIM-3, and integrated Human Cell Atlas reference datasets for comparison. CITE-seq profiling showed that TIM-3 was predominantly expressed on dendritic cells and NK cells, with variable expression across other populations, including CD34 cells and CD8 T cells. At baseline, we identified a population of CD34 myeloid-biased progenitors specific to MDS/CMML samples ("HSPC-like") characterized by inflammatory gene expression programs and features of impaired differentiation. In MDS, elevated baseline HLA class II expression across hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), HSPC-like cells, and multiple myeloid populations was associated with response. Consistent with this finding, trajectory analysis suggested that nonresponders bypassed HLA class II-high states during myeloid differentiation. In MDS, the presence of distinct CD8 T-cell populations and increased interferon-response programs in CD8 T and NK cells at baseline was also associated with response. In both MDS and CMML, treatment among responders was associated with contraction of BM CD8 and CD4 T-cell populations characterized by type I interferon-responsive and inflammatory programs, including IFIT1, IFIT2, and TNF, along with expansion of a distinct GZMH/IFITM1-expressing cytotoxic CD8 T-cell population. Together, these findings identify baseline antigen-presentation and immune-response programs associated with therapeutic response and reveal coordinated remodeling of myeloid and lymphoid compartments during azacitidine/sabatolimab treatment in MDS and CMML.

papers.title: Light-dependent conversion of body color change pattern during zebrafish development
papers.abstract: Zebrafish (Danio rerio) shows body color change in response to light: when light comes, it whitens body color. Our previous study has shown that larval zebrafish as early as 5 days post-fertilization (dpf) have this capacity fully developed whereas 2-dpf larvae exhibit light-induced darkening in sharp contrast (Shiraki et al. 2010). Here, we discovered that the conversion in body color change pattern between 2 dpf and 5 dpf is light-dependent: larvae reared in darkness exhibited light-induced darkening of body color, reminiscent of 2-dpf larvae. We also found that a 14-h light exposure on 3 or 4 dpf is sufficient to trigger this conversion, and that the conversion by light on 4 dpf still occurred after ablation of most exorh-expressing pineal photoreceptor cells. The dark-reared larvae had significantly lower transcription levels of pmch and pmchl, which encode melanin-concentrating hormone precursors, than the LD-reared larvae. However, the levels in larvae that had undergone the conversion (3-L and 4-L) were not significantly different from those in dark-reared larvae, indicating that the reduced pmch/pmchl expression alone does not account for the conversion. In conclusion, light exposure in rearing is indispensable for the maturation of body color change ability in larval zebrafish through a regulatory mechanism independent of exorh-expressing pineal photoreceptors.

papers.title: Ferroptosis of selective progenitor cell types during embryogenesis ensures proper organ morphogenesis
papers.abstract: Ferroptosis, a form of non-apoptotic cell death, is induced by lipid peroxidation resulting from an intracellular accumulation of labile iron (1). While apoptosis is involved in embryonic development (2), the role of ferroptosis in embryogenesis is unknown. Here, we report that the ferroptosis process occurs in the embryonic lung and kidney at mid- and late-gestation. In these tissues, pro-ferroptotic cells include subpopulations of the Sox9+ distal lung epithelial cells and the Flk1+ vascular progenitors in the kidney glomeruli. Lipidomic analysis reveals mixed lipid peroxidation as the driver for ferroptosis. The role of ferroptosis in the morphogenesis of these organs was confirmed by triple positivity of TfR1, 4-HNE and TUNEL, mitochondrial defects, cell membrane breakage, dead cell remnants, single-cell RNA-sequencing of a ferroptosis gene signature. Genetic manipulation of Gpx4, an endogenous inhibitor of ferroptosis. Further, genetic knockout or transgenic overexpression of Gpx4 affects lung and kidney development and results in cystic lungs and kidneys. Notably, conditional deletion Gpx4 results in hypoplasia of the lung epithelia and of the renal glomeruli, while transgenic overexpression of Gpx4 resulted in atelectasis with collapsed lung alveoli and hypertrophic glomeruli. Together, these findings show that ferroptosis regulates lung and kidney morphogenesis by acting in key progenitor cell populations during gestation. Supplementation of iron or polyunsaturated fatty acid during pregnancy has implications for organogenesis.

papers.title: Phenotypic and Molecular Characterization of Potentially New Shigella boydii Serotype in Bangladesh
papers.abstract: Objective: Shigella is a major cause of bacillary dysentery among children under 5 years of age, especially in low- and middle-income countries. At Dhaka hospital of icddr,b, every year around 3% of Shigella isolates from patients with diarrhea are identified as Shigella-like organisms (SLOs). These isolates do not react with any of the existing and provisional Shigella antisera. The major aims of the present study were to characterize a unique cluster of SLOs using phenotypic and genotypic methods. Methods: A cluster of 6 SLOs was characterized using biochemical tests, serotyping, antimicrobial susceptibility, and virulence assay by using the Sereny test, PCR and compared their pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) patterns with known serotypes of Shigella spp. Antisera against the isolate were raised in a rabbit model to determine cross-reactivity with known serotypes. Results: All six SLOs were mannitol fermenting, have invasive properties, positive for ipaH and Shigella enterotoxin 2 gene along with possession of virulence plasmid of ~ 140 MDa. All isolates were resistant to ampicillin, tetracycline, sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim, but were sensitive to mecillinam, nalidixic acid, and ciprofloxacin. Plasmid and PFGE profiles showed that the genomic patterns of these isolates were identical but were different from all other S. boydii serotypes. Antiserum prepared against one of the isolates agglutinated with all isolates but did not cross-react with other Shigella and E. coli reference strains. Conclusion: This unique cluster of isolates might belong to a new provisional serovar of S. boydii and further analysis is required to incorporate it into the stereotypic scheme of Shigella.

papers.title: The Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretome exerts antimicrobial activity against Burkholderia glumae by disrupting cell envelope homeostasis and impairing bacterial replication
papers.abstract: The effectiveness of antimicrobials used to manage bacterial infections is increasingly threatened by the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Many conventional antimicrobials act on a single defined target that pathogens can circumvent through target modification or pathway adaptation. In contrast, antimicrobials that disrupt multiple cellular processes may impose greater fitness costs and reduce the likelihood of resistance development, making their discovery a priority for pharmaceutical and agricultural applications. We previously demonstrated that the environmental bacterium Pseudomonas protegens PBL3 secretes a complex mixture of molecules (secretome) with antimicrobial activity against several plants and human pathogens. However, the mechanism underlying this activity remained unknown. Here, we used the plant pathogen Burkholderia glumae to investigate the mode of action of the P. protegens PBL3 secretome. We showed that the P. protegens PLB3 secretome causes extensive cell envelope damage that results in cell death and interferes with bacterial multiplication. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed broad disruption of processes associated with cell-envelope biogenesis and homeostasis and bacterial replication. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that the P. protegens PBL3 secretome acts as a multi-target antimicrobial that could be harnessed in the development of therapeutics to control bacterial infections of agricultural and medical importance.

papers.title: Long-read shotgun metagenomics identifies distinct urogenital microbial community states associated with functional potential and urinary tract infection during pregnancy
papers.abstract: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are among the most common bacterial infections during pregnancy and are associated with adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes. Although previous studies used enhanced culture, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and/or short-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize the urogenital microbiome of adult females, few have assessed the urogenital microbiome during pregnancy and thus this microbiome remains poorly understood. Here, we applied Oxford Nanopore long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing to characterize urogenital microbial composition, functional potential, metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), and the urogenital virome of pregnant females. Taxonomic profiling identified three distinct microbial community states predominated by Lactobacillus crispatus, Gardnerella species, and L. iners. The Gardnerella-predominated community was associated with a higher frequency of UTI during pregnancy. Functional profiles strongly reflected these community states, demonstrating that taxonomic differences were accompanied by distinct functional potential. Genome-resolved analysis recovered 415 MAGs, including 29 high-quality genomes, revealing substantial genomic diversity among urogenital microbes. Viral sequences, predominantly bacteriophages, also were detected in most samples, highlighting an additional component of the pregnancy-associated urogenital microbiome. These findings demonstrate that pregnant females possess distinct urogenital microbial community states and show that they differ not only in taxonomic composition but also in their functional potential.

papers.title: Fluorescence microscopic evidence for intracellular silicon storage pools in diatoms and their partial separation
papers.abstract: Diatoms are unicellular algae that occur ubiquitously in almost every salt- and freshwater habitat on earth. Silicic acid is taken up from the environment and stored in intracellular silicon storage pools (SSPs) to form species specific silica based cell walls (frustules). During biosilica formation in the silicon deposition vesicle (SDV), the silicon is transported from SSPs into the SDV. The present contribution describes the fluorescence microscopic visualization and quantification of silica solely formed from SSPs under silicon starvation. Labeling with the fluorescence marker PDMPO demonstrates continuing cell growth and cell division without silicon uptake from the environment. The SSPs of Cyclotella nana may account for up to 1/3 of total cellular silicon and intracellular concentrations up to ca. 540 mM, significantly beyond the saturation level (2 mM). The chemical state and localization of SSPs within cells are yet unclear. Here, we report a method for subcellular fractionation of C. nana by density gradient centrifugation. Quantification of cytoplasmic silicon yields 3 to 10% of the total cellular silicon corresponding to intracellular concentrations of ca. 50 to 160 mM. Labeling with NMR active 29Si shows that this silicon occurs as condensed silica, i.e., silicic acid is converted into condensed silica after uptake. However, the detected intracellular silicon concentrations are lower than the value of ca. 540 mM predicted by the fluorescence experiments. It is thus concluded that the missing SSP silicon is either present in the form of large aggregates or compartments. Alternatively, they may also be bound to cell wall biosilica.

papers.title: Genomic architecture of the major histocompatibility complex genes in the Neotropical Midas cichlid
papers.abstract: The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) plays a central role in vertebrate adaptive immunity, yet its genomic architecture remains poorly characterized in many evolutionary model systems, including the Neotropical Midas cichlid Amphilophus citrinellus. Here, we integrate chromosome-level functional genome annotation, transposable element (TE) profiling, transcriptomics, phylogenetics, molecular selection analyses, and protein structural modeling to characterize its MHC repertoire. We identified 298 MHC-related loci across 18 chromosomes, including 30 MHC-I genes, 15 MHC-IIA genes, and 20 MHC-IIB genes, together with antigen-processing and regulatory components. MHC-I and MHC-II genes were located on different chromosomes, consistent with the MHC non-linkage pattern characteristic of many teleosts. Gene duplication and phylogenetic patterns support birth-and-death evolution, resulting in a structurally diverse repertoire with broadly conserved protein domains. TE distribution varied across MHC genomic regions, suggesting a potential contribution to genomic diversification. Molecular selection analyses detected positive selection in MHC-I and IIB genes, whereas MHC-IIA showed more limited evidence of positive selection. Expression patterns varied across tissues, with relatively high expression of several MHC genes in the spleen and thymus, while structural models retained characteristic MHC folds. Phylogenetic analyses placed previously characterized MHC sequences with broader multilocus repertoire, suggesting that population level diversity may reflect both allelic polymorphism and variation among paralogous loci. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive chromosome-resolved characterization of the MHC repertoire in a Neotropical cichlid and establish a genomic framework for investigating immune gene diversification during the Midas cichlid radiation.

papers.title: Compartment-Resolved Matrisome Shifts During Postnatal Tendon Maturation in Mice
papers.abstract: Tendons acquire their load-bearing capacity during the first month of postnatal growth, driven by the extensive remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM). While the role of specific individual components to this process have been well characterized, a comprehensive assessment of how the tendon matrisome changes during this critical window is lacking. This, in part, is due to the challenges associated with solubilization of mature ECM, which is underrepresented by conventical proteomic approaches. To address this, we performed compartment-resolved proteomics on murine Achilles and plantaris tendons at postnatal days 0 (P0), P14, and P28. Sequential extraction methods leveraged a CHAPS-soluble fraction, capturing cellular and soluble matrisome proteins, from the insoluble mature ECM fraction, solubilized by guanidine hydrochloride and hydroxylamine hydrochloride and separately analyzed by label-free quantitative LC-MS/MS. Analysis shows that the two compartments followed distinct trajectories during maturation. The insoluble matrix was dominated by collagenous proteins, which increased from 95% to over 99% of the identified signal intensity, and its composition was largely established by P14. Within the soluble matrisome compartment, collagens increased from 50% to over 60% by P14, accompanied by dynamic regulation of proteins implicated in collagen processing (P4HA1, PCOLCE), crosslinking (LOX, LOXL2), and regulators of collagen fibril assembly and growth (DCN, BGN, FMOD, THBS3, THBS4). Beyond these established regulators, we observed dynamic regulation of less-characterized fibril-associated proteoglycans (KERA, OGN, CHAD), matricellular (COMP, POSTN, MATN2), and angiogenic regulatorily proteins (SERPINF1, ECM1). Together, this work establishes a comprehensive protein-level reference for postnatal tendon maturating, provides new insights into the molecular regulation of functional tendon development.

papers.title: Platycodin D2 Targets Vimentin to Suppress Fibroblast-Myofibroblast Transition: A Novel Therapeutic Strategy Against Pulmonary Fibrosis
papers.abstract: Background Pulmonary fibrosis is a progressive lung disease characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and irreversible decline in lung function with limited effective therapeutic targets. Vimentin, a type III intermediate filament protein, plays a critical role in fibroblast activation and fibrogenesis, representing a promising drug target. Methods Novel vimentin ligands were screened via virtual screening. SPR assay verified compound-vimentin binding affinity. CETSA and CD spectroscopy analyzed protein structural changes after compound binding. In vitro FMT model and in vivo bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis model were used to assess antifibrotic effects, and mutagenesis assays identified key binding amino acid residues. Results Platycodin D2 (PD2) from Platycodon grandiflorus was identified as a novel high-affinity vimentin ligand (Kd = 392.8 nM). PD2 binds vimentin directly, alters its secondary structure and induces insoluble aggregation. It effectively inhibits TGF-{beta}1-induced FMT in vitro and mitigates bleomycin-induced pulmonary fibrosis in vivo, reducing collagen deposition and improving animal survival. Critically, mutagenesis validation confirmed that key residues (Glu138 in chain A, Glu132 and Glu143 in chain B, as well as Glu50 and Arg54 in chain C) are essential for this interaction. Conclusions Our findings establish PD2 as a novel pharmacological inducer of aberrant vimentin aggregation, presenting a distinct target-driven strategy for antifibrotic drug development.

papers.title: Diversification of budding yeast polarization dynamics after compensatory experimental evolution
papers.abstract: Essential cellular processes evolve under strong selection, yet protein networks underlying conserved functions can vary substantially. To what extent evolution constrains the intracellular dynamics of proteins performing essential functions is currently largely unknown. Here, we characterize budding yeast polarization phenotypes along a previously established evolutionary recovery trajectory, compensating for the loss of near-essential polarity gene BEM1. Through quantitative live cell imaging, we show that loss of BEM1 weakens and destabilizes polarization. Surprisingly, in recovered evolved lineages, protein dynamics change significantly compared to the ancestor: most notably, presence of main regulator Cdc42-GTP is strongly decreased, while polarisome member Spa2 localizes more slowly into mobile foci. Although separate phenotypic characteristics are only weakly constrained, we find evidence of effective protein-independent localization modes, revealing signs of convergence along the evolutionary trajectory. Together, our results show that evolution can restore global cellular function without conserving microscopic organization, instead giving rise to novel molecular phenotypes.

papers.title: Physiological mapping and prediction reveal stress-responsive translation initiation landscapes
papers.abstract: Translation initiation defines the protein output of the transcriptome, but its physiological dynamics in cells and tissues remain incompletely characterized. Here we develop TISCA2, an inhibitor-free method that captures eIF5B-associated initiating ribosomes to map translation initiation sites genome-wide. By directly identifying start sites rather than inferring translation from elongating-ribosome periodicity, TISCA2 improves the detection of short and overlapping translons. Translation of a subset of TISCA2-identified translons is supported by N-terminal proteomics and HLA-I immunopeptidomics. The arsenite-induced integrated stress response broadly redistributes start-site usage, reducing upstream initiation in favor of downstream initiation. TISCA2 further reveals tissue-specific initiation landscapes in vivo, with increased detection of downstream candidate start sites in the testis. Finally, we develop IncepTIS, a sequence-based deep learning model that predicts position-resolved and condition-dependent initiation landscapes. IncepTIS-guided optimization generates de novo mRNA 5' leaders with stress-responsive initiation patterns. Together, TISCA2 and IncepTIS provide an experimental and computational framework for mapping, predicting and engineering translation initiation in mammalian cells and tissues.

papers.title: Gut Roseburia hominis-derived 10-hydroxystearic acid alleviates metabolic disorder by restoring hepatic fatty acid metabolism
papers.abstract: Metabolic disorders and health-promoting dietary interventions represent complementary contexts of metabolic impairment and improvement, providing an opportunity to identify gut microbial taxa associated with both disease status and dietary response. Here, we integrated five independent human cohorts spanning metabolic disorders and dietary interventions and identified Roseburia hominis as a gut microbial taxon that consistently decreased in metabolic disorders and increased after dietary interventions. Beyond species abundance, strain-level genetic variation in R. hominis provided additional information for distinguishing metabolic disorder status and stratifying cardiometabolic severity. Integration of phenotype-associated variants with circulating metabolomics prioritized ohyA, encoding an oleate hydratase, as a candidate functional determinant linking R. hominis genetic variation to host metabolic heterogeneity. An ohyA-based genetic burden score was associated with adverse cardiometabolic traits and changed longitudinally during dietary intervention, while circulating metabolites statistically accounted for part of the associations between ohyA variants and host phenotypes. Functional experiments demonstrated that R. hominis OhyA protein converts oleic acid to 10-hydroxystearic acid (10-HSA), whereas an OhyA carrying five prioritized missense substitutions showed markedly impaired enzymatic activity. In high-fat diet-fed mice, 10-HSA attenuated body-weight gain, improved glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity, and reduced dyslipidemia and hepatic steatosis. Multi-omics profiling revealed limited remodeling of the gut microbiota but pronounced hepatic transcriptional and metabolic responses, characterized by activation of PPAR-associated lipid-metabolic pathways, altered fatty-acid oxidation and desaturation, and remodeling of hepatic lipid composition. Together, these findings establish a diet-responsive R. hominis-OhyA-10-HSA axis linking microbial variation to host metabolic dysfunction and show that 10-HSA can improve metabolic health in mice.

papers.title: BCL10 Gain-of-Function Impairs Germinal Center Participation by Naive B Cells and Cooperates with BCL6 to Drive Extrafollicular Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
papers.abstract: BCL10 gain-of-function (GoF) mutations occur in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) cases of the BN2/C1 molecular subgroup. These alterations activate CARD11-BCL10-MALT1 (CBM) signaling and drive resistance to multiple drug classes, but their role in disease pathogenesis is incompletely understood. In particular, interactions between BCL10 GoF and additional DLBCL oncogenes are undefined. Here, we show BCL10 GoF in naive B cells blocks their participation in germinal center (GC) reactions and permits transformation to DLBCL with a non-GC B-cell phenotype. Most clinical cases with BCL10 GoF also carry translocation of the BCL6 proto-oncogene, and we show that co-activation of these two lesions together promotes pronounced oncogenic synergy. Detailed single-cell analyses of underlying premalignant B-cell populations revealed expansion of extrafollicular memory B cells whose gene-expression program remains prominent in resulting lymphomas in both the mouse and corresponding human tumors. We therefore define a novel role for BCL10 activating mutations in enabling BCL6 lymphomagenesis.

papers.title: How Fisherian runaway halts: Genomic architecture determines the long-term evolutionary consequences of sexual selection.
papers.abstract: Sexual selection explains the evolution of exaggerated sexual displays, but less obvious is why biased mate preferences--a requirement for sexual selection--evolve. Fisher (1930) proposed that biased mate preferences can spark self-reinforcing evolutionary process (runaway) that drives their own evolution. This occurs because mate choice imposes sexual selection on sexual displays and links them genetically to mate preferences, producing indirect selection on the preferences themselves. While mathematical models have demonstrated the plausibility of the runaway theory, they rely on several idealized assumptions. Consequently, it remains poorly understood how runaway halts once populations deviate from these idealized conditions as a consequence of evolution via runaway, and how the genetic architecture underlying sexual displays influences the resulting evolutionary dynamics. Here, we address these gaps using two complementary approaches. First, we review and synthesize existing theories to classify the mechanisms that halt runaway into four categories, based on which idealized assumptions of Lande's (1981) classic model are violated during evolution via runaway. Second, we conduct individual-based evolutionary simulations varying the genetic architecture of sexual displays from conventional additive to omnigenic inheritance models. Our results show that genetic architecture determines how runaway process halts, thereby governing long-term evolutionary dynamics under sexual selection.
